name: Software engineering: programming by example for string transformations (SyGuS-Comp PBE strings)
description: Write a synthesiser that, from a few input-output examples and a grammar, returns a string-manipulation program (phone numbers, names, initials, university addresses) that also reproduces held-out examples of the same task. The score is the fraction of 27 SyGuS-Comp tasks solved.

sources.locator: Gulwani (POPL 2011): FlashFill, synthesising string transformations in spreadsheets from input-output examples.
Alur et al. (FMCAD 2013): syntax-guided synthesis, the problem format (grammar plus specification) of these tasks.
Alur, Radhakrishna and Udupa (TACAS 2017): EUSolver, enumerative synthesis with divide and conquer, evaluated on SyGuS PBE string tasks.
Padhi, Millstein, Nori and Sharma (CAV 2019): overfitting in synthesis, programs that fit the examples but not the intended function.
Pinned SyGuS benchmarks (no licence stated): the base and '-long' files of the 27 tasks.

requirements.datasets: SyGuS-Org/benchmarks PBE_SLIA_Track/from_2018 at commit 13c8deb6 (no licence stated; fetched from the pinned URL and not redistributed), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py.

evaluation.benchmark: Software engineering: programming by example for string transformations (SyGuS-Comp PBE strings)
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: synthesize(task) -> str. task = {'name': str, 'function': str, 'params': [[name, sort], ...], 'sort': 'String', 'start': nonterminal, 'grammar': [[nonterminal, sort, [productions]], ...], 'examples': [[[argument strings], output string], ...]} is a SyGuS PBE string problem: productions are parameter names, literals (string literals as {'str': value}, integers, true, false), other nonterminals or operator lists such as ['str.substr', 'ntString', 'ntInt', 'ntInt']. Return one SMT-LIB term (an S-expression string; string literals in double quotes with "" for a quote, negative numbers as -1 or (- 1)) that the grammar derives from 'start'. Operations follow SMT-LIB 2.6 string semantics (str.++, str.len, str.at, str.substr, str.indexof, str.replace, str.to.int, int.to.str, str.prefixof, str.suffixof, str.contains, +, -, =, ite, with the edge cases of the standard, e.g. out-of-range str.at and str.substr give "" and str.to.int of a non-numeral gives -1). A task is solved when the term reproduces the given examples and the held-out examples of the benchmark's '-long' variant. Score: fraction of the 27 tasks solved, maximised; a term that does not parse or leaves the grammar counts as unsolved, a non-str answer makes the evaluation invalid. synthesize() is called once per task, all tasks in one sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 120 s CPU in total, 2 GB); it should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks).

limitations: Only 27 tasks, from a few families (11 phone-number tasks, 4 name-combination tasks, 6 university-address tasks and 6 others), so scores move in steps of 1/27 and families are correlated.

Correctness is judged on examples: the given ones plus 8 to 94 held-out examples of the '-long' variant per task (3 to 94 distinct ones, because the long files repeat examples; bikes has 3); a program that agrees on all of them but differs elsewhere counts as solved.

SyGuS-Comp scored consistency with the given examples and solving time, not generalisation, so published solved counts are not comparable; the benchmark repository notes that errors and duplicates may exist.
The bottom-up enumeration seed solves 8 of 27 within its budget; the tasks are public and solutions could be remembered, which the contract excludes but cannot check.

The interpreter implements the SMT-LIB 2.6 string semantics used by SyGuS-Comp 2018 and was cross-checked against Z3 on random terms; a solver with different edge-case semantics could disagree on unusual programs.

state_of_the_art.statement: No published value measures generalisation to the held-out '-long' examples of these 27 tasks; the bottom-up enumeration seed solves 8 (computed here).

sources.title: Overfitting in Synthesis: Theory and Practice

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Programming by example: synthesise a program in a given language that maps the example inputs to their outputs and generalises to the user's intended transformation.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Most spreadsheet and data-wrangling users cannot program; synthesis from examples (FlashFill and its successors) automates such transformations, and finding a program that generalises from a few examples, rather than one that merely fits them, is the central difficulty.

papers.title: Automating string processing in spreadsheets using input-output examples
papers.primary_goal: Synthesise string-manipulation programs from a few input-output examples for spreadsheet users.
papers.task_relation: The task asks for such programs for string transformations of the same kind.

papers.title: Scaling Enumerative Program Synthesis via Divide and Conquer
papers.primary_goal: Make enumerative syntax-guided synthesis scale to larger programs and example sets.
papers.task_relation: The task's problems are SyGuS PBE string tasks of the kind EUSolver was evaluated on.

papers.title: Overfitting in Synthesis: Theory and Practice
papers.primary_goal: Understand and reduce overfitting of synthesised programs to the given examples.
papers.task_relation: The task scores generalisation to held-out examples, i.e. the absence of overfitting.
